title: The Manager Who Was Too Good at His Job
author: The Mindful Manager
summary: The Mindful Manager takes Todd Jackson's metaphor of the umbrella manager, who shields the team from organisational noise, and the funnel manager, who passes everything down, and argues that treating them as a binary is a mistake. Using the image of an overprotective parent who follows children around the playground, the author warns that umbrella management leaves people unable to cope once the manager leaves. A story of a manager whose team collapsed after he departed is used to show how protection can become dependency. The author proposes a third model, the sieve, which lets the right things through, holds the rest back and requires judgement. Practical guidance includes asking whether holding something back protects the team or just the manager from an awkward conversation, and filtering rather than hiding. The closing line is that a leader's goal is to make themselves unnecessary.
points: The umbrella and funnel metaphor is useful in context but becomes a trap when treated as a complete leadership model.
Over-protective managers create dependency, as shown by a team that collapsed and left after its umbrella manager departed.
The sieve manager lets the right information through, holds back the rest and translates what needs translating, which takes judgement.
A key test is whether holding something back protects the team or merely protects the manager from an awkward conversation.
The ultimate goal of leadership is to make yourself unnecessary by helping people navigate the organisation without you.
quotes: Umbrella managers shield a team from the endless stream of requests, distractions and shifting priorities coming from above, allowing them to focus more efficiently on the work. Funnel managers simply pass them on.
The problem comes when people take this out of context and start treating it as a complete leadership model, as if managers have to be one or the other.
The sieve neither blocks everything nor passes everything through. It lets the right things through, holds the rest back and, crucially, requires judgement.
If you go on holiday or leave the company and your team collapses, you didn’t do your job.

One of the main responsibilities of a manager is to develop the managers of tomorrow, the future leaders of the company. You can’t do that if you don’t let them experience the organisation as it is, the good and the bad.
When issues arise, ask yourself one question first: does holding this back protect my team, or does it just protect me from an awkward conversation?
Caring for someone isn’t about doing everything for them and building them an easy life. It’s about empowering them to learn and grow, without becoming their safety net.
Because the ultimate goal of leadership isn’t to make yourself indispensable.
